rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 3.1-3.2, Tables 1-2, Figs 9-13 - the study reports its own data from the SIAR advisory service: advised net irrigation depths averaged over three or more seasons in three pilot areas, estimates of farmer adherence by pilot area, and results of 875 field evaluations of drip, solid-set sprinkler and center-pivot systems (emission uniformity, working pressure, CU).
rows.notes: The study is a descriptive account of an irrigation advisory service (SIAR) in Castilla-La Mancha, not a study of on-demand irrigation networks. It never evaluates on-demand networks or measures water-use inefficiency attributable to them or to lack of scheduling. The nearest statements are general: distribution networks must deliver required flows timely 'for any type of water delivery scheme', and adherence to advice varies with 'type of distribution network' among other factors (Section 3.1), with low adherence in Tajo-basin areas where water is paid by surface rather than volume. It reports on-farm system uniformity and pressure problems, and asserts SIAR improves water use, but gives no measured result on the claimed effect (on-demand networks causing inefficient water use without adequate scheduling). Hence Q2 is no; the claim is an inference the review draws, not a finding of this study.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is primarily a programme description with observational summary data (advised depths, adherence estimates, system evaluation statistics); it contains no experiment or comparison concerning on-demand delivery networks.
